title: Integrated Security & Compliance Playbook: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence & Exceptions
author: Ava Martinez
body:
Summary:
This playbook consolidates Redwood Inference's controls and operational procedures for: RBAC & authentication, audit logging, data residency & retention, secure SDLC practices, incident response (security-focused), compliance evidence generation, and risk/exception handling. It is intended for system owners, platform engineers, security reviewers, and compliance leads.

Scope:
- Applies to all Redwood-managed control plane components, hosted API endpoints, Dedicated control plane, and Private deployment artifacts (control plane configs and packaging).
- Excludes third-party SaaS that is covered by vendor contracts unless explicitly integrated with our production identity or audit systems.

Principles:
- Least privilege by default: grant the minimum role for tasks and require just-in-time elevation where possible.
- Immutable evidence: audit logs and compliance artifacts must be tamper-evident and retained per policy.
- Defense-in-depth: pair RBAC with strong authentication (SSO, MFA) and continuous monitoring.
- Measurable controls: instrument SLOs, alerting, and periodic reviews for each control area.

Section 1 - RBAC & Authentication
1.1 Roles and role mapping:
- Platform roles (high-level): organization-admin, security-admin, infra-operator, svc-account, dev, readonly.
- Service-specific roles: runtime-admin, model-onboarder, billing-analyst, observability-reader.
- Mapping guidance: map SSO groups to platform roles with group-scoped assignments; prefer group provisioning (SCIM) over per-user grants.

1.2 Authentication standards:
- Primary identity provider: Okta (OIDC + SCIM). Secondary: Google Workspace for contractors where provisioned.
- Require MFA for all human accounts with access to production (OKTA policy: MFA required, push preferred).
- Service accounts: use short-lived tokens (vault-issued) for ephemeral work; no long-lived API keys without an exception.

1.3 Access lifecycle and reviews:
- Onboarding: template-based access requests via Access Requests (GitHub issue + Jira ticket) with approver chain (manager -> owner_team -> security).
- Quarterly access reviews: owners must certify role assignments; SRE and security run automated discrepancy reports.
- Deprovisioning SLA: 24 hours for terminated employees; immediate for security incidents.

1.4 Example RBAC matrix (roles -> capabilities):
| Role | Read Config | Deploy | Manage Secrets | Query Audit Logs | Approve Exceptions |
|------|-------------|--------|----------------|------------------|--------------------|
| org-admin | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| infra-operator | yes | yes | limited | yes | no |
| dev | yes | limited | no | no | no |
| readonly | yes | no | no | no | no |

Section 2 - Audit Logging
2.1 What to log:
- Authentication events: login success/failure, SSO token issuance, MFA events.
- Authorization decisions: role assignments, policy evaluations, access denials.
- Admin actions: deploys, model pinning, rollout changes, config modifications.
- Data access: read/write operations against customer-sensitive stores (object storage, DBs).
- System changes: infra changes, scaling events, OS-level privileged accesses.

2.2 Logging architecture:
- Agents: Fluentd (edge) -> central Kafka (clustered) -> immutable cold store (S3 with versioning + Glacier lifecycle).
- Primary SIEM: Splunk (indexed for 365 days hot, 730 days warm), with subset forwarded to long-term archive for 7 years for compliance customers.
- Integrity: logs are hashed on ingestion (SHA-256) and checkpoints are stored in KMS-wrapped manifests.

2.3 SLOs and alerts:
- Logging ingestion latency: 99th percentile < 60s.
- Missing-log alert: if expected heartbeat or control-plane audit events absent for > 5 minutes -> P1 to oncall-sre.
- Suspicious activity alert thresholds: >5 failed auth attempts in 10m for an account, >50 role grants in 1h by an individual account.

2.4 Retention policy (summary):
- Authentication & authorization events: 3 years (hot/warm per compliance tier).
- Admin/config changes & deploys: 5 years.
- Data access logs for production customer data: per-customer retention policy (default: 1 year), honored by data-residency tag.

Section 3 - Data Residency & Retention
3.1 Controls by data class:
- Metadata (non-PII, telemetry): multi-region storage allowed; default region us-west-2. Retention: 2 years.
- Customer data (model inputs/outputs that are customer-identifiable): region-locked (per contract) and tagged at ingestion. Retention: contract-defined, default 1 year.
- Audit & evidence artifacts: stored per retention table in Section 2.4 and encrypted at rest.

3.2 Enforcement mechanisms:
- Ingestion tags: every request that stores customer data must include residency_tag and retention_ttl headers enforced by the API gateway and validated by sidecar policy.
- Storage policies: S3 bucket policies + object-level encryption with KMS keys scoped per region/customer where required.
- Proof-of-residency report: automated quarterly report generated for customers with residency requirements.

Section 4 - Secure SDLC (Secure Development Lifecycle)
4.1 Stages & requirements:
- Design: threat models and data-flow diagrams required for services handling sensitive data.
- Build: dependency scanning (Snyk/OSS scanning), static analysis (Semgrep, Trivy), and container image attestations.
- Test: unit/integration tests + security tests; fuzzing for parsers and model input paths.
- Release: require pull request template fields for security review, binary signing, and canary rollout plan.
- Post-release: automated canary monitoring, SLA validation, and regression checks against quality guardrails.

4.2 Gate checklist (PRs touching prod-facing code):
1) Threat model updated (if scope changed).
2) Dependency vulnerabilities <= critical fixed or approved exception.
3) Unit tests coverage threshold met (team baseline).
4) Security review sign-off (security engineer or designated reviewer).

Section 5 - Incident Response (Security Procedures)
5.1 Incident classification:
- Sev 1 (P0): confirmed data exfiltration, production compromise, or control-plane encryption key exposure.
- Sev 2 (P1): suspected credential compromise, broad-service degradation with security indicators.
- Sev 3 (P2): isolated non-production issues or low-impact exposures.

5.2 Immediate playbook (first 60 minutes):
1) Triage: oncall-sre and security oncall join incident bridge.
2) Contain: rotate service tokens associated with compromise (Vault), and isolate affected nodes/pods.
3) Preserve evidence: snapshot affected hosts, preserve logs (make immutable copies to archive location).
4) Communicate: notify incident channel and executive oncall per severity.

5.3 Forensics & evidence handling:
- Chain of custody: log actions taken, artifact hashes, investigator names, and timestamps.
- Forensic storage: segregated S3 bucket with restricted access and write-once-lock where supported.

Section 6 - Compliance Evidence Workflows
6.1 Evidence catalog and owners:
- Access logs (Owner: infra-observability).
- Vulnerability scans & SCA reports (Owner: eng-sre/security).
- Pen test reports (Owner: security).
- Policy exception approvals and meeting minutes (Owner: governance-compliance).

6.2 Evidence request process (external auditor or customer):
1) Request submitted to /security-evidence request queue (Jira).
2) Evidence owner validates scope and prepares sanitized artifacts.
3) Evidence delivered via secure share (S3 pre-signed link with expiration) and logged.
4) Post-delivery: auditor feedback captured and remediation tracked.

6.3 Artifact templates included:
- Log manifest (hashes + retention metadata).
- Environment snapshot (versions, deployed images, config hashes).
- Access certification export (CSV of role assignments at time T).

Section 7 - Risk & Exception Handling
7.1 Exception policy (when a control cannot be met):
- Exception submission: template describing control, compensating controls, risk impact, and mitigation timeline.
- Approvers: owner_team lead -> security -> governance board (for high-impact exceptions).
- TTL & renewals: exceptions expire after 90 days by default and require evidence of mitigation to renew.

7.2 Risk acceptance matrix (summary):
- Low: dev-only features with compensating controls - owner_team approval.
- Medium: production-facing with limited blast radius - security + owner_team.
- High: material customer or regulatory impact - governance board and exec sponsor.

Operational Ownership & Contacts:
- Security: security@redwood.example.com (oncall rota via PagerDuty).
- Infra & Observability: eng-sre@redwood.example.com.
- Compliance/Governance: compliance@redwood.example.com.

Appendices:
A. Example Incident Evidence checklist (quick reference)
- Preserve logs (S3 path) and copy to forensic-bucket.
- Export access list snapshot (CSV).
- Rotate affected secrets and document KMS access.
- Record timeline: start, detection, containment, eradication, recovery.

B. Templates & CLI snippets
- Generate log manifest:
  aws s3api list-objects --bucket redwood-audit-archive --prefix prod/2029-01- --query 'Contents[].{Key: Key, ETag: ETag}'

C. Revision history:
- 2028-01-10: Created by Ava Martinez.
- 2028-06-01: Added SIEM retention profiles and hash manifest guidance.
- 2029-01-15: Updated retention defaults and incident containment SLA; published.

If you are an owner of a control referenced here but see a gap or outdated procedure, open a ticket in the security playbook backlog and assign to security@redwood.example.com.
